headline: Chips drag a second week lower as TSMC's capex shock meets a Chinese AI challenge, leaving the S&P 500 at 7,457 (prior cash close) while gold holds near $4,017 overnight.
stance: The market is digesting two simultaneous blows to the AI trade: TSMC's record Q2 beat was overshadowed by a ~15% capex-budget increase ($60–64 bn) that spooked investors about cost inflation across the chip supply chain, and a new Chinese AI model (Moonshot/Kimi) renewed fears that hyperscaler spending could decelerate. The S&P 500 posted its worst weekly decline in over a month (–1.6%), with the Nasdaq off –2.9%, yet underlying credit and liquidity gauges remain calm — this looks more like a tech-valuation reset than a broad macro deterioration. The Fed holds at roughly 90% odds of no change on July 29; the real risk is a September hike re-pricing if Middle East oil pressure keeps inflation sticky.

news.head: TSMC capex shock
news.body: TSMC reported Q2 EPS of $4.31 (beat vs $4.26 consensus) and Q3 revenue guidance of $44.6–45.8 bn (+37% YoY), but raised 2026 capital spending to $60–64 bn from prior guidance of $52–56 bn, plus pledged an additional $100 bn Arizona investment — the capex jump sent the stock down ~7% on the week and pulled the entire semiconductor complex lower.

news.head: Chinese AI model rattles chip trade
news.body: Chinese startup Moonshot AI (Kimi) unveiled a new model it says narrows the gap with leading US AI offerings, reigniting fears that hyperscalers may dial back AI infrastructure spending, compounding the chip-sector selloff.

news.head: Netflix sinks on weak outlook
news.body: Netflix fell more than 10% on Friday after Q2 revenue of $12.56 bn narrowly missed consensus of $12.6 bn and the company's Q3 guidance came in below expectations on both earnings and revenue.

news.head: Middle East escalation lifts oil
news.body: Ongoing US strikes on Iranian targets and Iran's retaliations in the region kept Strait of Hormuz risk elevated, pushing WTI crude to a prior cash close of $81.77/bbl (Brent $88.09) and amplifying concerns that sticky energy prices could force the Fed to hike in September.

news.head: June inflation data mixed but dovish tilt
news.body: Headline CPI fell 0.4% in June and final-demand PPI fell 0.3%, which all but removed a July Fed hike from the table (~90% probability of no change at the July 29 meeting), though resilient retail sales (+0.2%) and initial jobless claims at 208K kept the 'soft-landing vs. stagflation' debate alive.

news.head: Trump-China tension resurfaced
news.body: President Trump claimed China interfered in the US 2020 election, threatening the tariff truce established last year and adding a fresh geopolitical overlay to equity risk.

implications: The semiconductor sector faces a 'good news is bad news' earnings season: strong demand proof (TSMC beat) is being offset by ballooning capex commitments that raise return-on-investment questions across the AI supply chain.

Sticky oil above $80/bbl (WTI) and above $88 (Brent) — both at roughly the 79th–85th percentile of 3-year ranges — keep September Fed-hike risk alive despite benign June CPI/PPI; real rates at 2.31% already weigh on growth-stock valuations.

Rotation away from chips toward financials, industrials, and energy continues; the S&P 500 equal-weight index held better than the cap-weighted index, suggesting the selloff is concentrated rather than broad.
Gold (prior cash close $4,023/oz; overnight ~$4,017) is being capped by elevated real rates and a firmer dollar even as geopolitical risk is high — a classic 'high-rate vs. safe-haven' standoff.

Hyperscaler earnings next week (starting with Alphabet) are the make-or-break moment for the AI trade: a capex-spending confirmation would stabilize chips; any pull-back language could extend the selloff.

Positioning: In rates futures, speculators have almost no bullish bets left on 3-month SOFR (2nd-percentile — a contrarian floor). In equities, speculators have almost no bullish bets left on Russell 2000 futures (2nd-percentile — a contrarian floor for small caps). In FX, speculators have almost no bullish bets left in British pound (2nd-percentile) and are modestly extended short in euro (12th-percentile) — both contrarian floors. In commodities, speculators are heavily positioned in copper (94th-percentile) — a contrarian warning given copper already sits at the 96th-percentile of its 3-year price range.

watch.head: Alphabet earnings (next week)
watch.body: Alphabet's Q2 report is the next major read on whether hyperscaler AI capex is accelerating or stalling — the single most important near-term catalyst for chip stocks.

watch.head: Fed July 29 decision
watch.body: Markets price ~90% odds of no change; any hawkish surprise or September-hike signaling in the statement could reprice risk assets sharply.

watch.head: Strait of Hormuz / Iran
watch.body: Any escalation toward an actual shipping chokepoint closure would spike Brent toward $90+ and re-ignite the stagflation trade (higher oil, lower growth stocks, flight to short-duration).

watch.head: Copper positioning vs. price
watch.body: Copper at $6.27/lb sits at the 96th price-percentile while speculators are extended long at the 94th positioning-percentile — a contrarian warning; watch for a break below $6.00 if risk-off deepens.

watch.head: USD/JPY at extreme
watch.body: The yen at 162.35/$ sits at the 99th percentile of its 3-year range — a historically extreme level; any de-escalation or dovish Fed pivot could trigger a sharp yen reversal that hits US equity flows.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: 10Y Treasury yield: 4.55% (prior cash close); 2Y: 4.18% — curve is +37 bps (10Y minus 2Y), positive but flat, consistent with a 'higher-for-longer' Fed rather than imminent easing.

Real rates at 2.31% are restrictive and cap gold and long-duration equity valuations; the 10Y breakeven inflation sits at 2.24%, implying the bond market still trusts the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility.

June headline CPI fell 0.4% and PPI fell 0.3% — two months of disinflation — but retail sales (+0.2%) and jobless claims (208K, a very low level historically) signal the economy hasn't buckled under high rates.

The Fed's balance sheet is growing only 1.26% year-over-year; overnight reverse repo (the parking facility for excess cash) has essentially drained to $0.1 bn — meaning liquidity is coming from bank reserves ($3,143 bn) not from the Fed injecting new money.

Term premium (the extra yield investors demand to hold long bonds vs. rolling short ones) is 77.9 bps — elevated, meaning the bond market is charging a meaningful risk premium to lend to the US government long-term.
ISM manufacturing at 53.3 (above 50 = expansion) and ISM services at 54.5 both signal the US economy is still growing, complicating the case for early rate cuts.

CAPE ratio (a measure of how expensive stocks are relative to 10 years of earnings) sits at 41.52 — well above historical averages — leaving equities with little margin for error if rates stay high or earnings disappoint.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left on 3-month SOFR interest-rate futures (2nd-percentile of 3 years, the lowest in that window) — a contrarian floor suggesting the rates market may be over-pricing hike risk.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: S&P 500 prior cash close: 7,457.69 (–1.01% Thursday); NDX prior cash close: 25,520.24 (–1.4%); DJIA prior cash close: 52,146.42 (–0.77%) — all three indices posted weekly losses of 1.6%, 2.9%, and 0.9% respectively.
The PHLX Semiconductor index is on track for a 20% decline from recent highs as TSMC's capex shock ($60–64 bn 2026 budget, up ~15%) spread to Nvidia (–2%), Micron (–4%+), and Intel on the week.
Netflix fell more than 10% Friday (revenue miss, weak Q3 guide), adding consumer discretionary/streaming to the list of earnings-season casualties.

Breadth is mixed but not broken: 68.2% of S&P 500 members trade above their 50-day average and 70.1% above their 200-day average (as of Jul 16) — the index is being dragged by a handful of mega-cap tech names, not a broad collapse.

VIX (the S&P 500 fear gauge) closed at 18.77 (prior cash close) — elevated relative to the calm of early 2026 but not at panic levels (below 20); VXN (Nasdaq fear gauge) is higher at 29.03, reflecting concentrated tech stress.
SKEW index at 147.3 signals that options traders are paying up for tail-risk protection (i.e., hedging against a larger, sudden drop) — a sign of caution beneath the surface calm.

The equity risk premium (the extra return stocks offer above risk-free bonds) is negative at –2.05% — stocks are not offering a cushion over Treasuries at current valuations, making the index particularly rate-sensitive.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left in Russell 2000 small-cap futures (2nd-percentile of 3 years, with specs and hedgers at opposite extremes) — a contrarian floor for small caps if risk sentiment stabilizes.

single_name.note: Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) — the world's dominant AI-chip foundry — reported a record Q2 profit (+77% YoY net income) and beat earnings estimates, yet the stock dropped ~7% on the week as the market focused on a 15% capex-budget increase and warnings that overseas fab expansion will compress gross margins 3–4% in coming years; large off-exchange block buying (quiet institutional accumulation) and a burst of unusual options activity were flagged in the scan, with company insiders having bought recently — shorts require ~1.8 days of average volume to cover (low squeeze risk), suggesting the post-earnings drop may be a valuation-reset opportunity rather than a fundamental break.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: HY-IG spread (the gap between junk-bond and investment-grade yields, a stress barometer) is 271 bps — elevated but not alarming; investment-grade spreads at 78 bps are similarly benign, suggesting corporate credit markets have not yet caught the equity-tech jitters.

Commercial paper funding spread (a short-term corporate borrowing cost gauge) is only 29 bps — near-normal, meaning even lower-rated companies can still borrow cheaply in the short-term money markets.

FRA-OIS and SOFR-OIS spreads (interbank stress gauges — roughly, 'does any bank fear lending to another bank overnight?') are both at –1 bps — essentially zero stress in the plumbing of the financial system.
Bank credit growth is running at 5.98% year-over-year (as of Jul 8) and loan syndication yields are 6.96% — credit is still flowing, but at a price that reflects the high-rate environment.

The Chicago Fed's National Financial Conditions Index at –0.535 and the St. Louis Fed's Financial Stress Index at –0.88 both signal that overall financial conditions remain loose (below zero = easier than average) despite the tech selloff.

Bank reserves are $3,143 bn — ample; overnight reverse repo has drained to just $0.1 bn, meaning excess liquidity that was parked at the Fed has been fully deployed into the market, removing a former buffer but also removing a passive drag on risk assets.
M2 money supply is growing at 5.58% year-over-year — a steady pace that supports nominal spending but also keeps the Fed cautious about declaring victory on inflation.

single_name.note: Scorpio Tankers (STNG) — a product-tanker operator — sits at the intersection of elevated oil/energy credit and Middle East shipping risk; large off-exchange block buying and a burst of unusual options activity are live, with 2 insider buying rules fired and the stock trading above its 200-day line; shorts need ~2.2 days of average volume to cover (modest squeeze risk). Signal is aging at ~50% weight.
